title: Operational and Economic Conditions for Electrified Trailers in Battery Electric Long Haul Transport
content: An electrified trailer adds battery capacity and a driven axle to a truck combination, potentially reducing dependence on public charging while increasing vehicle mass and energy demand. This paper develops an analytical framework for determining when that trade-off can reduce transport costs. We analyse our vectotool route simulation results for Aachen–Rosenheim, Madrid–Antequera and Stockholm–Arvidsjaur, with exploratory extensions to heavier combinations. The distinction between total electricity demand, public charging demand, charging-related delay and full ownership cost is maintained throughout. For the Madrid case, the reported energy consumption increases from 122 to 164 kWh per 100 km, while public charging decreases from 512 to 182 kWh. A reconstructed electricity-cost calculation gives a saving of approximately EUR 85 per tour at the stated tariffs, consistent with the reported EUR 84. The Stockholm case similarly reports higher energy consumption and lower energy expenditure, but its driving duration exceeds ten hours and cannot demonstrate ordinary single-driver daily feasibility. A sensitivity run with a larger and faster-charging reference tractor leaves the electricity saving almost unchanged on both routes, while the dwell advantage on the Stockholm route falls from 126 to 40 minutes. We therefore distinguish a cost mechanism, which is robust to the tractor, from a time mechanism, which acts as a schedule-feasibility constraint and depends on the tractor and on national working-time law. The analysis identifies a conditional economic mechanism rather than universal superiority: avoided public charging expenditure and realizable time benefits must exceed additional capital, energy, infrastructure and payload costs. The results support this mechanism but are neither independently validated nor statistically representative of European freight operations.
